content: The primary treatment for visceral leishmaniasis (VL) in East Africa involves the parenteral administration of pentavalent antimonials and paromomycin for a duration of 17 days. For complicated cases, liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) is used as a second-line treatment, administered at a daily dose of 3–5 mg/kg over 6–10 days, with a total cumulative dose of 30 mg/kg. First-line combination therapy is generally effective and safe in patients without HIV. However, in patients co-infected with HIV, treatment options are more limited due to higher rates of toxicity and parasitological failure. HIV-positive VL patients often require higher doses of paromomycin and L-AmB. When L-AmB was administered at a total dose of 30 mg/kg to HIV-positive patients, the cure rate was 60%, compared to 93% in HIV-negative patients. Increasing the dose to 40 mg/kg improved the cure rate to 74% in first VL episodes but only 38% in relapse cases, with failure rates of 16% and 56%, respectively. A retrospective analysis in Ethiopia showed a 43% cure rate with sodium stibogluconate in VL-HIV patients, but this drug is known to be highly toxic in HIV-infected individuals. Monotherapy with any drug has shown limited efficacy in this population. However, a retrospective study demonstrated that co-administration of L-AmB (30 mg/kg total dose) and miltefosine in VL-HIV patients resulted in significantly higher cure rates (84%) and lower failure rates in both primary and relapsed cases. Combination therapy with L-AmB and miltefosine should be further evaluated to improve treatment outcomes and delay the onset of treatment resistance. Relapse rates in VL-HIV co-infected patients are higher than in HIV-negative individuals, but this is difficult to quantify due to poor follow-up. Relapse risk is particularly high in patients with low CD4 cell counts (<200 cells/μL), multiple previous VL episodes, lack of antiretroviral therapy (ART), or failure to achieve clinical or parasitological cure during the first VL episode. Secondary prophylaxis is generally targeted at those at the highest risk of relapse. Monthly pentamidine, though not used as a treatment for VL in East Africa, has been studied as a relatively safe prophylactic option. In South-East Asia, particularly in India’s Bihar state, VL has been endemic for over a century and is co-endemic with HIV. Although the overall incidence of VL has been declining, 7–20% of reported VL cases in adults are co-infected with HIV, with significant district-level variation. Improved surveillance and routine HIV testing for VL patients may have contributed to the increased detection of co-infection. In Nepal, 1–5% of VL patients were found to be HIV-positive, and sporadic cases of VL-HIV co-infection have been reported in Thailand. The diagnostic and treatment challenges of VL-HIV co-infection in East Africa are also present in South-East Asia. Outcomes of treating VL in HIV-positive patients in India with higher doses of L-AmB are better than those observed in East Africa but remain worse than in HIV-negative patients. Late recognition of co-infection is common, as not all VL patients are systematically offered HIV testing. Many co-infected patients present with severe morbidity and low CD4 cell counts (<200 cells/mm³). In Bihar, where economic migration is high, screening HIV-positive individuals for VL in non-endemic areas has been recommended, especially for those who have spent significant time in VL-endemic regions. Tuberculosis (TB) is an emerging concomitant infection in VL-HIV co-infected patients in India. The combined immunosuppressive effects of VL and HIV increase the risk of reactivating latent TB infections, leading to triple infections. VL-HIV patients are more likely to develop disseminated TB, which is harder to diagnose and may contribute to persistently high mortality rates. Up to 20% of VL-HIV patients with pulmonary symptoms have been diagnosed with TB using nucleic acid amplification tests. These patients are at the highest risk of mortality, and managing treatment for VL, TB, and HIV simultaneously presents significant challenges. The pathogenesis of VL and HIV involves complex mechanisms of immune dysregulation. Both infections multiply in myeloid or lymphoid cells, leading to impaired cellular (Th1) and humoral (Th2) immune responses. Active Leishmania infection induces prolonged Th2 activation in HIV-positive patients, increasing viral replication and further depleting CD4 cell counts. The Th1 response, mediated by interleukin-2, interleukin-12, and interferon-γ, is critical for macrophage activation and intracellular parasite killing. In contrast, a predominance of Th2 cytokines, such as interleukin-4 and interleukin-10, is associated with progressive disease. VL-HIV co-infected patients often present with atypical symptoms, including localized parasite detection in abnormal tissues (e.g., intestine, oral cavity, skin, lungs), which can be misdiagnosed as flare-ups of underlying diseases. The clinical overlap between advanced HIV/AIDS and VL further complicates diagnosis. Differentiating VL symptoms from those of disseminated mycobacterial infections, lymphoma, or histoplasmosis is essential. Skin manifestations of leishmaniasis are more common in HIV-positive patients and may occur before, during, or after a VL episode. These manifestations can include parasite dissemination, atypical lesions, and even visceralization. The gold standard for VL diagnosis and cure assessment remains direct parasite visualization via microscopy of tissue aspirates (spleen, bone marrow, or lymph nodes). Molecular tests, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), are highly sensitive but require specialized resources and are not yet validated as replacements for parasitological methods. There are no specific guidelines for treating VL in HIV co-infected patients in regions where VL is caused by Leishmania donovani. Combination therapy has been encouraged due to its potential advantages, including better efficacy, lower toxicity, reduced risk of drug resistance, shorter treatment duration, and improved compliance. However, clinical trials are challenging due to the dispersed geographic distribution of cases and low rates of HIV testing in VL patients. Secondary prophylaxis is ideally initiated after a negative test of cure, but in regions with anthroponotic transmission, drugs used as firstor second-line therapy are not recommended for prophylaxis due to concerns about resistance development. The WHO has recommended innovative policies for using drug combinations and limiting monotherapy to L-AmB where possible. Combination regimens are being tested for their potential to improve treatment outcomes and reduce toxicity. Current guidelines focus on VL-HIV co-infection management in East Africa and South-East Asia, while recommendations for other forms of leishmaniasis and regions with Leishmania infantum remain unchanged.
